Chapter 28

The capture page

Wiring the form into markup, showing validation errors accessibly, hiding a honeypot properly, the one page that cannot be prerendered — and what a visitor sees when the server fails.

By the end of this chapter

A working, accessible signup form.

The // … and <!-- … --> lines stand for what this listing leaves out: the other imports and the page data, the hero copy column beside the form, and — inside the form — the experience <select> and the consent checkbox (the same field pattern again), the honeypot, which the next section shows, and the comments the real file puts above each part.

What the spreads do

  • {...requestGuide} on the <form> — sets action, method and the enhancement handler. Without JavaScript this is an ordinary POST that works; with JavaScript it submits in the background.
  • {...requestGuide.fields.email.as('email')} on the input — sets name, type, aria-invalid and the value binding. as() accepts every HTML input type: text, email, password, number, date, checkbox, radio, file, select, and more.
  • requestGuide.pending — a counter of in-flight submissions. Disabling on it prevents the double-submit you get from an impatient double-click on a slow connection.

role="alert" on the error paragraph makes a screen reader announce the message the moment it appears, rather than only when the user happens to navigate onto it. aria-describedby then links the error to the input, so focusing the field re-reads it.

aria-invalid is set for you by field.as(…), so we style the error state off the same attribute assistive technology reads. One source of truth — the visual and the announced state cannot disagree.

Hiding the honeypot correctly

  • Off-screen, not display: none. Sophisticated bots skip display: none fields precisely because they know it is a trap.
  • tabindex="-1" — keyboard users never land on it.
  • aria-hidden="true" — screen readers never announce it.
  • autocomplete="off" — this is the one people miss. Without it a password manager fills the field in and flags a real person as a bot, silently rejecting genuine signups.

The 16px rule

iOS Safari automatically zooms the page when you focus an input whose font-size is under 16px — and it does not zoom back out. Users experience this as your site breaking when they tap a field. It is one of the most common mobile bugs on the web and the fix is one line.

This page cannot be prerendered

Run a build now and it fails:

Why

A remote form() builds its own action attribute from the current request URL, so a submission returns you to the page you submitted from with any query string intact. Prerendering happens at build time, where there is no request and therefore no meaningful URL — so SvelteKit throws rather than baking in a wrong one. The rule: a page hosting a remote form must be server-rendered.

The cost is small. This page renders per request instead of being a static file, adding a few milliseconds of server time. Everything expensive about it — CSS, fonts, JavaScript — is still static and still cached at the edge. Only the HTML shell is dynamic.

When the server fails

Every failure so far has an answer the visitor can act on. A field the schema rejects comes back as an issue beside that input, and too many attempts comes back as an issue on the email field. What is left is the failure nobody planned: the disk the leads are written to is full, or there is a bug, and leadStore.has() or save() throws before the handler reaches its redirect().

When code on the server throws, SvelteKit does not send the exception to the browser. It reduces every error to a small object of type App.Error, which always has two fields: a status (an HTTP status code such as 404 or 500) and a message. The reducing is done by a hook called handleError — a function SvelteKit calls for every error, which you may export from a file named src/hooks.server.ts. StrikeFlow has no such file, so SvelteKit's built-in default applies, and it does two things. An error the code threw on purpose, like the error(404, 'No article found at …') in the blog route, keeps the status and the sentence it was given. Anything else — an exception nobody planned — is printed to the server's console with its full stack, and reaches the browser as { status: 500, message: 'Internal Error' }.

Why the real message never reaches the browser

Because an unplanned error is, by definition, one nobody has checked is safe to show. Ours would read something like ENOTDIR: not a directory, open '/srv/app/package.json/leads.jsonl' — a file path on the server, handed to anyone who submits the form. Database errors can carry worse: table names, fragments of queries, sometimes credentials. SvelteKit's errors documentation puts it plainly: unknown errors "can contain sensitive information", so "unknown error messages and stack traces are not exposed to users". The full error goes to the server's log, where you can read it; the visitor gets a safe sentence. If you want a friendlier one than 'Internal Error', that is what your own handleError is for:

That is an option, not part of StrikeFlow. Once you supply the hook, logging is your job — SvelteKit only logs unknown errors itself when you have not. The errors documentation covers the rest, including adding fields such as a support reference to App.Error.

Where does the visitor see that App.Error? The documentation for remote forms answers: "If an error occurs during submission, the nearest +error.svelte page will be rendered." +error.svelte is a route file, like +page.svelte, and SvelteKit walks up the folders from the failing route looking for one. With none anywhere, it falls back to a page of its own, which is this short:

A status code and a message, and nothing else: no heading a person would write, no way back to the form, not even a title. It is a safety net, not a page you ship. So StrikeFlow has its own, at the root of src/routes, where it catches every route on the site:

  • error arrives as a prop, typed as ErrorProps from ./$types — the same way a page receives data. Older code reads page.error from $app/state, as the built-in page does, and that still works; the prop is the SvelteKit 3 idiom, because the component then depends on its inputs rather than on global state.
  • It renders inside the root layout, so the header, footer and skip link stay, and the two buttons give the visitor somewhere to go.
  • error.message is shown as it stands, because handleError has already made it safe: either the sentence the code wrote, or 'Not Found' / 'Internal Error'. The heading carries the human words, by status.
  • No <Seo>: an error page has no canonical URL to claim. It gets a title and noindex, and SvelteKit sends it with the real status code — a 404 is a 404, not a 200 page that says not found.

Why the capture page catches nothing itself

Because it has nothing better to say. The failures that reach this point are ones the visitor cannot fix by changing what they typed, and the only safe sentence about them is the one handleError has already written. A catch in the page would be code for the one case with no better message to show, so we let the error page take it. The cost is real and worth naming: the error page replaces the form, and a visitor who wants another go has to come back to it — which is why our error page offers the way back. For three fields that is a fair trade. For a long form it is not: take control of the submission with enhance, and read the next warning before you do.

A catch around a remote call receives a different shape. Await form.submit() inside enhance — or a command() in a click handler — and a failure rejects with SvelteKit's HttpError: { status, body }, where body is that same App.Error. It is not an Error, and it has no message of its own. So (error as Error).message is undefined, and error instanceof Error ? error.message : 'Something went wrong' throws the server's sentence away every time — while a plausible sentence sits on screen and nothing looks broken. Read body.message, behind isHttpError(). A <svelte:boundary>'s failed snippet and +error.svelte are the other way round: they receive the App.Error itself, so they read error.message.

Look at the condition. isHttpError(error) narrows the type, so error.status and error.body.message need no cast. Then error.status !== 500 separates the two kinds of message: any other status was chosen by code — a 503 because signups are paused, a 429 from a rate limiter — and came with a sentence meant for a person, while 500 is what every unplanned error becomes, and its 'Internal Error' would sit under the form like a shrug. Those, and anything that is not an HttpError at all, get one sentence of our own.

We checked both shapes in a real browser before writing them down, against a lead store that could not be read and an error(503, …) added for the experiment. Left to the error page, the 503's own sentence — Signups are paused while we move the list. — reached the visitor, and the store failure arrived as Internal Error. The same two failures caught in enhance arrived with error instanceof Error false, error.message undefined, and the server's words in error.body.message. The store failure is pinned by e2e/failure.e2e.ts, with JavaScript and without (chapter 36 shows how).

Checkpoint

Submit the form with a bad email and see an inline error. Submit a good one and land on /guide/thank-you?t=…. Then disable JavaScript in devtools and do it again — it should still work. Last, watch it fail: set LEADS_DIR in your .env to package.json — a file where the store expects a folder — restart pnpm dev and submit. You get the site's error page, Something went wrong over Internal Error, inside the header and footer, and the ENOTDIR error with its stack in the terminal. Put LEADS_DIR back afterwards. While you are there, visit /no-such-page: the same component, saying it can't find the page, with a real 404 status in the network tab.
